document.title: AlexNet – The Model That Sparked the Deep Learning Boom
document.description: A look into AlexNet, the breakthrough CNN that won ImageNet 2012 and changed the trajectory of deep learning.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation If LeNet was the blueprint, AlexNet was the explosion. In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton entered the ImageNet competition with a deep CNN. The result shocked everyone: their model crushed the competition with a top-5 error of 15.3% compared to the next best at 26.2%. That’s not just a win, that’s a landslide. This single result is what most people point to as the moment that started the modern deep learning boom. For me, it was also the first "big" CNN I read about after LeNet. It showed me that the same ideas could scale up if you had enough data and enough compute. Back then, GPUs weren’t commonly used for neural networks. AlexNet was the first to really lean on GPUs for training, and that’s what made it possible to train a network this large. ## Model Breakdown AlexNet is much bigger than LeNet, but it’s not complicated once you see the pattern. Here’s a layer-by-layer look: - **Input:** 224×224 RGB image from ImageNet (1000 classes). - **Conv1:** 96 filters of size 11×11, stride 4 → 55×55 feature maps. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **Conv2:** 256 filters of size 5×5. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **Conv3:** 384 filters of size 3×3. - **Conv4:** 384 filters of size 3×3. - **Conv5:** 256 filters of size 3×3. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **FC1:** 4096 units. - **FC2:** 4096 units. - **Output:** 1000 units with softmax. So compared to LeNet, AlexNet just stacks more convolution layers and makes them wider. One thing you might notice in some AlexNet diagrams is that the architecture looks split into two parallel streams. That wasn’t a design choice for accuracy — it was because the model was too large for a single GPU in 2012, so the authors divided it across two GPUs and linked them at certain layers. ## Why the Design Choices Matter **ReLU activations** Instead of tanh, AlexNet used ReLU. This made training much faster because ReLU doesn’t saturate in the positive domain. Today ReLU (or its variants) is the default. **Dropout** The fully connected layers had dropout, which randomly turns off some neurons during training. This was a clever way to reduce overfitting. **Data augmentation** They trained with random crops and flips of images. That might sound basic, but it was a big deal at the time because it helped the model generalize better. **GPUs** AlexNet was split across two GPUs because a single one couldn’t handle the full model. This parallelization was another first for deep learning. ## Implementation Notes Here’s a PyTorch version of AlexNet that matches the original design: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class AlexNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes=1000): super(AlexNet, self).__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 96, kernel_size=11, stride=4, padding=2), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), nn.Conv2d(256, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(384, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(384, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), ) self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(256 * 6 * 6, 4096), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, 4096), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Linear(4096, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), 256 * 6 * 6) x = self.classifier(x) return x ``` When I trained this on a subset of ImageNet, the model quickly became computationally heavy compared to LeNet or even smaller CNNs. It made me appreciate just how critical GPUs were for the success of AlexNet. Without them, the training time would have been completely unrealistic. ## Reflections Reading about AlexNet made me realize how much of progress in deep learning comes down to scaling. The ideas weren’t brand new. Convolutions, pooling, and fully connected layers were already there in LeNet. What AlexNet added was size, data, GPUs, and a few clever tricks like ReLU and dropout. After AlexNet, things snowballed. VGG showed that depth with small filters could work even better. GoogLeNet focused on efficiency with inception modules. ResNet solved the vanishing gradient problem with skip connections. But if you trace back all of those, AlexNet was the model that kicked the door open.

document.title: Fast R-CNN — Making Detection Practical
document.description: Breaking down Fast R-CNN (2015), which introduced ROI Pooling and end-to-end multi-task training, making object detection far faster and more accurate than the original R-CNN.

body.raw:
## Context & Motivation

R-CNN had proven a big point: deep CNN features were far
better than hand-crafted ones for object detection. On
PASCAL VOC, it nearly doubled the mean average precision
compared to Deformable Parts Models (DPMs). But while the
accuracy was great, the system itself was a mess.

The biggest pain point was **speed**. For each image,
Selective Search proposed about 2000 regions, and the CNN
had to be run separately on every single one. Processing a
single image could take minutes. That made R-CNN
impressive as research, but unusable in practice.

The second issue was **multi-stage training**. First you
fine-tuned the CNN. Then you froze it and trained SVMs on
the features. Then you trained bounding box regressors.
Finally, you stitched everything together at test time. It
worked, but it wasn’t elegant, and storing all those CNN
features on disk could take hundreds of gigabytes.

So by 2015, the question was: how do we keep the accuracy
but get rid of the inefficiencies? The answer came in the
form of **Fast R-CNN**, which reorganized the pipeline
around two key ideas:

1. Run the CNN **once per image**, not once per region.  
2. Train the classifier and regressor **end-to-end**, with
   a single multi-task loss.

Those two changes made Fast R-CNN dramatically faster,
cleaner, and easier to train. It pushed object detection
closer to being practical outside the lab.


## Main Idea of Fast R-CNN

The key insight behind Fast R-CNN was simple: stop wasting
time. Instead of running the CNN thousands of times on
warped proposals, **run it once on the whole image** and
then reuse that shared feature map for all proposals.

Here’s how the pipeline looks compared to R-CNN:

1. The full image is passed through a CNN (in the paper,
   VGG16 was the main backbone). This produces a **feature
   map** for the entire image.  
2. Region proposals (still from Selective Search) are
   projected onto this feature map. Instead of cropping and
   warping raw pixels, we now crop from the feature map.  
3. A new trick called **ROI Pooling** converts each region
   of interest into a fixed-size feature (like 7×7). This
   means no more stretching objects into 227×227 squares.  
4. These fixed-size pooled features go through a few fully
   connected layers.  
5. From there, the network branches into two heads:  
   - A **softmax classifier** that predicts the object
     category (or background).  
   - A **bounding box regressor** that refines the box
     coordinates.  

The whole system is trained **end-to-end** with a single
multi-task loss:

- **Classification loss:** softmax cross-entropy.  
- **Localization loss:** smooth L1 regression loss.  

This solved two of R-CNN’s biggest problems in one shot:
- Computation was shared — the CNN ran once per image, not
  2000 times.  
- The pipeline was unified — no more SVMs, no more feature
  caching, no more separate regressors.  

With these changes, Fast R-CNN ran orders of magnitude
faster than R-CNN and even improved accuracy. It showed
that object detection could be efficient *and* accurate,
setting the stage for the next leap: Faster R-CNN.


## Architecture Breakdown

Fast R-CNN kept the same overall goal as R-CNN — find
objects and draw boxes around them — but restructured the
pipeline to be faster and more elegant. Let’s walk through
it piece by piece.

---

### Step 1: Full-Image CNN Feature Map

In R-CNN, each region proposal was cropped from the image,
resized to 227×227, and passed through a CNN separately.
That meant thousands of CNN forward passes per image —
incredibly slow.

Fast R-CNN flipped this idea. Instead of cropping first,
it runs the CNN **once on the entire image**. The output is
a **convolutional feature map** (for example, with VGG16
you get a feature map that’s about 1/16th the size of the
input).

This was the big efficiency gain. All the heavy lifting
of convolution happens only once. The proposals will
reuse this shared feature map instead of raw pixels.

---

### Step 2: Region Proposals on the Feature Map

Fast R-CNN still relied on **Selective Search** to generate
about 2000 candidate regions. The difference was what
happened next.

Instead of cropping the proposals directly from the raw
image (like in R-CNN), Fast R-CNN **projects them onto the
CNN feature map**. Each proposal corresponds to a rectangle
on the feature map, since the map is spatially aligned
with the input image.

This change looks small, but it removed the need to resize
and warp every proposal into 227×227 images. Instead, all
proposals are just slices of the shared feature map —
lighter, faster, and less distorted.

To see how projection works, let’s walk through an
example with real numbers.

Suppose our input image is **224×224 pixels**. After
passing through VGG16 (used in the Fast R-CNN paper), the
final convolutional feature map is **14×14** in spatial
resolution. Why? Because VGG16 has pooling layers that
downsample by a factor of 2 at five different stages:
2⁵ = 32. So the feature map is roughly 1/16 the size of
the input.

Now imagine Selective Search proposes a bounding box:
(x=32, y=64, w=96, h=128). This is in the coordinates of
the original image.

To map this box onto the feature map, we divide all values
by the downsampling factor (16 in this case):

- x = 32 ÷ 16 = 2  
- y = 64 ÷ 16 = 4  
- w = 96 ÷ 16 = 6  
- h = 128 ÷ 16 = 8  

So the corresponding region on the feature map is a box at
(x=2, y=4) with size (6×8). This is the **projection step**:
the proposal box from the image becomes a rectangle on the
feature map.

From here, ROI Pooling will take that 6×8 patch and convert
it into a fixed grid (say 7×7) so it can go into the fully
connected layers.

### Step 3: ROI Pooling

Here’s the challenge: after projection, each region
proposal corresponds to a rectangle on the shared feature
map. But these rectangles are all different sizes. Some
might cover a 6×8 patch, others might be 3×3, others 12×14.
Fully connected layers, however, expect a fixed-size input.

R-CNN solved this by **warping each region to 227×227**
before feeding it to AlexNet. Fast R-CNN replaced that
with a new operation: **ROI Pooling**.

How ROI Pooling works:

1. Each region of interest (ROI) is projected onto the
   feature map (like we saw in the last step).  
   Example: a box covering a 6×8 patch.  
2. This patch is divided into a fixed number of bins, say
   **7×7**. That means the 6×8 area is split into 49 bins.  
3. Inside each bin, we perform **max pooling**. No matter
   how many values are inside a bin, it’s reduced to one
   number.  
4. The result is a **7×7 grid of pooled values**. Each ROI,
   no matter its original size, now produces the same
   fixed-size output: 7×7×C (where C is the number of
   channels in the feature map, e.g., 512 for VGG16).

So in our example, a 6×8 patch becomes exactly 7×7 after
ROI Pooling. Another ROI, maybe 12×14, would also shrink
to 7×7. This allowed Fast R-CNN to handle variable-sized
regions **without any distortion**.

Why it mattered:
- No more warping raw pixels.  
- Computation stayed on the feature map (cheaper).  
- Output was fixed-size, so the same FC layers could
  process any ROI.

---

### Step 4: Fully Connected Layers and Outputs

Once each ROI has been pooled into a fixed 7×7×C feature,
we can flatten it and pass it through fully connected
layers. In the Fast R-CNN paper, they used VGG16, so after
ROI Pooling each proposal was fed into two fully connected
layers with 4096 units each.

At the top, the network **splits into two heads**:

1. **Classification head:**  
   - A softmax layer predicts the probability of each class
     plus one extra class for “background.”  
   - Example: for PASCAL VOC (20 categories), the softmax
     has 21 outputs.  
   - This replaces the SVMs used in R-CNN.

2. **Bounding box regression head:**  
   - A regressor predicts 4 numbers (Δx, Δy, Δw, Δh) for
     each class.  
   - These are offsets that adjust the ROI to better match
     the object.  
   - Unlike R-CNN, this regressor is trained jointly with
     the classifier, not separately.

Together, these two heads make Fast R-CNN **end-to-end**.
Instead of training a CNN, then SVMs, then regressors in
different stages, everything is optimized at once with a
**multi-task loss**.

### Step 5: Multi-task Loss

The final innovation in Fast R-CNN was how it trained the
two outputs — classification and bounding box regression —
**together in a single objective**. This was called the
**multi-task loss**.

---

#### 1. Classification Loss
For each region of interest, the network predicts a class
label from `K+1` categories: one for each object class
(e.g., 20 in PASCAL VOC) plus one for “background.”  

The classification head outputs a probability vector `p`
of length `K+1`. The ground truth label is a number `u`
(0 = background, 1 = aeroplane, …, 20 = tvmonitor).

The loss here is just **softmax cross-entropy**:
L_cls(p, u) = -log(p_u)


This penalizes the model if it assigns low probability to
the true class.

---

#### 2. Localization Loss
If the region is a foreground object (not background), we
also want the bounding box regressor to improve the box
coordinates. For each class, the regression head predicts
4 numbers: `t = (tx, ty, tw, th)`.

The ground truth box is parameterized in the same way,
`v = (vx, vy, vw, vh)`. The regression target is the
difference between proposal and ground truth, normalized
for scale.

The loss used here is the **Smooth L1 loss**:
L_loc(t, v) = Σ smooth_L1(t_i - v_i)


Why Smooth L1?  
- L2 loss is too sensitive to outliers (big errors blow up
  the gradients).  
- L1 loss is stable but not smooth.  
- Smooth L1 combines the best of both: quadratic for small
  errors, linear for big ones.  

---

#### 3. Combining the Two
The final multi-task loss for one ROI is:

L(p, u, t, v) = L_cls(p, u) + λ [u ≥ 1] L_loc(t, v)


- `L_cls(p, u)` = classification loss.  
- `L_loc(t, v)` = localization loss.  
- `[u ≥ 1]` is an indicator function — we only apply the
  bounding box loss if the ROI is a foreground object.  
- λ is a balancing factor (set to 1 in the paper).

This meant the network could **learn both tasks at the same
time**, end-to-end. Unlike R-CNN, there was no need for
separate SVMs and regressors. Everything was optimized
together.

---

#### Why It Mattered
- Unified training = simpler pipeline.  
- Classification and localization reinforced each other.  
- Faster and more accurate than the stitched-together R-CNN
approach.  

This multi-task loss design carried forward into almost
every detector that came after Fast R-CNN, from Faster
R-CNN to modern architectures.

## Why the Design Choices Matter

What makes Fast R-CNN so interesting is that it didn’t
invent a brand-new idea out of nowhere. Instead, it took
the messy pieces of R-CNN and reorganized them into a
pipeline that was both faster and cleaner. Each design
choice directly addressed a specific weakness of R-CNN.

---

### Shared Convolutional Features
- **Problem in R-CNN:** the CNN had to run separately on
  ~2000 regions per image. This made detection painfully
  slow.  
- **Fast R-CNN’s solution:** run the CNN once on the whole
  image, then reuse that feature map for all proposals.  
- **Why it mattered:** suddenly, the bottleneck shifted
  from “minutes per image” to something much closer to
  real time. The computational waste was gone.

---

### ROI Pooling
- **Problem in R-CNN:** region proposals came in different
  shapes and had to be warped to 227×227, causing
  distortion and wasted computation.  
- **Fast R-CNN’s solution:** ROI Pooling mapped proposals
  onto the shared feature map and pooled them into a fixed
  size (e.g., 7×7).  
- **Why it mattered:** variable-sized proposals became
  standardized *without* warping, and computation stayed
  inside the network. ROI Pooling became a building block
  that lasted until ROI Align (Mask R-CNN).

---

### End-to-End Multi-task Training
- **Problem in R-CNN:** training was split into stages:
  fine-tune CNN → extract features → train SVMs → train
  regressors. Each step was separate and required storing
  huge feature sets on disk.  
- **Fast R-CNN’s solution:** a single network with two
  heads (classification + regression), trained jointly with
  a multi-task loss.  
- **Why it mattered:** no more SVMs, no more feature
  caching. The detector became trainable in one pass,
  directly optimizing for detection performance.

---

### Smooth L1 Loss for Localization
- **Problem in R-CNN:** bounding box regression used simple
  linear regression, which could be sensitive to outliers.  
- **Fast R-CNN’s solution:** Smooth L1 loss, which is
  stable for large errors but precise for small ones.  
- **Why it mattered:** better localization and more stable
  training.

---

Together, these choices turned R-CNN’s proof of concept
into something practical. Fast R-CNN was still tied to
Selective Search for region proposals, but by removing the
computational and training bottlenecks, it showed that CNN
detectors could be both accurate and efficient. This
paved the way for the next step: Faster R-CNN.


## Implementation Notes

Fast R-CNN is easier to explain if we build it piece by
piece. The main difference from R-CNN is that the CNN runs
once per image, and then region-specific features are
pulled out with ROI Pooling. Let’s walk through it in
steps.

---

### Step 1: Shared Feature Map Extraction

We start with a CNN backbone (VGG16 in the original
paper). Instead of running it 2000 times per image, we run
it once and keep the convolutional feature map.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torchvision.models as models

# VGG16 backbone, keep only convolutional layers
vgg16 = models.vgg16(weights=models.VGG16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)
backbone = nn.Sequential(*list(vgg16.features.children()))


Now, passing an image through backbone gives us the
shared feature map that proposals will reuse.

### Step 2: Region Proposals

Fast R-CNN still used Selective Search for proposals.
We can reuse the code from the R-CNN section that returns
boxes (x, y, w, h) in image coordinates.

The only difference is that now we will project those
boxes onto the feature map. If the feature map is 1/16
the size of the input image, we divide all coordinates by
16.

```python 
def project_boxes(boxes, stride=16):
    # boxes = [(x, y, w, h), ...] in image coordinates
    projected = []
    for (x, y, w, h) in boxes:
        projected.append((
            int(x / stride),
            int(y / stride),
            int(w / stride),
            int(h / stride)
        ))
    return projected
```

### Step 3: ROI Pooling

Now comes the key innovation. We take each projected box
on the feature map and turn it into a fixed-size tensor,
say 7×7, regardless of the box size.

PyTorch has this implemented in torchvision.ops:

```python
from torchvision.ops import roi_pool

# feature_map: [N, C, H, W]
# boxes: list of tensors [num_boxes, 5] (image_idx, x1, y1, x2, y2)
pooled = roi_pool(feature_map, boxes, output_size=(7, 7))
```

- Each ROI is cropped from the feature map.
- It is divided into a grid (7×7).
- Max pooling inside each cell reduces it to a fixed-size
feature.

So no matter if the original proposal was 6×8 or 12×14,
after ROI Pooling we always get a 7×7×C tensor.

### Step 4: Fully Connected Layers

Once ROI features are fixed size, we flatten them and pass
them through fully connected layers (like in VGG).

```python
class FastRCNNHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, num_classes):
        super(FastRCNNHead, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_channels * 7 * 7, 4096)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4096, 4096)
        self.cls_score = nn.Linear(4096, num_classes)   # softmax
        self.bbox_pred = nn.Linear(4096, num_classes * 4)  # bbox regression

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.flatten(start_dim=1)
        x = torch.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = torch.relu(self.fc2(x))
        scores = self.cls_score(x)
        boxes = self.bbox_pred(x)
        return scores, boxes
```
Here:
- cls_score predicts class probabilities (softmax).
- bbox_pred predicts 4 offsets for each class.

### Step 5: Multi-task Loss

Finally, we train both heads together using the multi-task
loss:

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F

def fast_rcnn_loss(scores, boxes, labels, targets, lambda_=1.0):
    # Classification loss
    cls_loss = F.cross_entropy(scores, labels)

    # Localization loss (Smooth L1), only for foreground ROIs
    pos = labels > 0
    loc_loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(
        boxes[pos], targets[pos], reduction="sum"
    ) / labels.numel()

    return cls_loss + lambda_ * loc_loss
```

This combines softmax cross-entropy for classification
with Smooth L1 for bounding box regression.

### Putting It All Together
So the Fast R-CNN workflow looks like this:
1. Run the CNN backbone once to get the feature map.
2. Project proposals onto the feature map.
3. Apply ROI Pooling to get fixed-size features.
4. Pass pooled features through fully connected layers.
5. Output class probabilities + bounding box refinements.
6. Train the whole system end-to-end with multi-task loss.

Compared to R-CNN, this design eliminated redundant CNN
computations, removed SVMs, and replaced warping with ROI
Pooling. The result was a detector that was both faster
and more accurate.

## Reflections and What Came Next

What I find striking about Fast R-CNN is how much of a
“cleanup job” it feels like. R-CNN had already shown that
CNN features were powerful for detection, but the system
was slow, clunky, and stitched together in multiple stages.
Fast R-CNN didn’t invent something totally new; instead, it
fixed the exact bottlenecks that were holding R-CNN back.

- **Shared computation** turned detection from minutes per
  image into something much closer to real time.  
- **ROI Pooling** solved the distortion problem of warping
  proposals.  
- **Multi-task training** simplified the pipeline into a
  single end-to-end system.  

For me, the big lesson here is how progress often happens:
not by giant leaps, but by carefully identifying pain
points and removing them one by one. Fast R-CNN showed that
a detector could be both accurate *and* efficient, and that
set the stage for the next step.

Of course, one major bottleneck still remained: **Selective
Search**. Even though the rest of the system was fast,
region proposals were still computed with a slow, hand-
crafted algorithm. Fixing that would be the next leap, and
it came quickly in the form of **Faster R-CNN**, where the
region proposal network (RPN) finally replaced Selective
Search.

Fast R-CNN isn’t widely used today, but its fingerprints
are everywhere. ROI Pooling, multi-task loss, and the idea
of end-to-end detection training carried forward into
almost every detector that followed.

document.title: GoogLeNet – Going Deeper with Inception
document.description: Exploring GoogLeNet (Inception v1), the 22-layer network that won the 2014 ImageNet Challenge with fewer parameters and a novel module design.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation By 2014, VGG had shown that just stacking more layers worked, but it came with a huge cost — VGG16 had 138 million parameters, which made it slow and heavy. The team at Google came up with a smarter idea. What if instead of making everything deeper and wider, we let the network decide which filter size works best at each stage? That’s where the **Inception module** came in. GoogLeNet (also called Inception v1) introduced this clever building block, which made it possible to go **22 layers deep** but with only about 5 million parameters. And with it, they won the ImageNet 2014 challenge with a top-5 error of just 6.7%. --- ## Architecture Breakdown The core of GoogLeNet is the **Inception module**. Each module has four parallel paths: - 1×1 convolution (cheap, fast, reduces dimension) - 3×3 convolution (captures mid-size features) - 5×5 convolution (captures larger features) - 3×3 max pooling (adds robustness) The outputs from all these paths are concatenated along the depth dimension, which means the network can look at multiple receptive field sizes at once. To make this efficient, they used **1×1 convolutions** before the expensive 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions. These acted like bottlenecks, reducing the number of channels and cutting down computation. Instead of finishing with big fully connected layers like AlexNet and VGG, GoogLeNet used **global average pooling** before the final softmax. This cut down parameters and reduced overfitting. ### High-level flow: Input (224×224) → Conv + Pool → Multiple Inception modules stacked → Global Average Pooling → Softmax classifier --- ## Why the Design Choices Matter **Inception module** This was the star of the show. It let the network capture small, medium, and large patterns all at once, which made it more flexible. **1×1 convolutions** They might sound useless, but they reduce the number of channels before bigger convs, acting like “compression.” This saved a ton of compute. **Global average pooling** This replaced huge fully connected layers with a simple average of each feature map. It massively reduced parameters (5M vs 138M in VGG16). **Auxiliary classifiers** GoogLeNet also added small classifiers in the middle layers to help with training. These acted like extra gradient signals. You don’t see this much today, but it was useful at the time. --- ## Implementation Notes Here’s a simplified version of an Inception block in PyTorch: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class InceptionModule(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, f1, f3_in, f3_out, f5_in, f5_out, pool_proj): super(InceptionModule, self).__init__() self.branch1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, f1, kernel_size=1) self.branch3 = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels, f3_in, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(f3_in, f3_out, kernel_size=3, padding=1), ) self.branch5 = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels, f5_in, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(f5_in, f5_out, kernel_size=5, padding=2), ) self.branch_pool = nn.Sequential( nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(in_channels, pool_proj, kernel_size=1), ) def forward(self, x): b1 = self.branch1(x) b3 = self.branch3(x) b5 = self.branch5(x) bp = self.branch_pool(x) return torch.cat([b1, b3, b5, bp], 1) ``` This modular design made it possible to build very deep networks without having to blow up the number of parameters. When I tried coding it, the Inception module felt surprisingly elegant: each branch is simple, but the concatenation at the end gives it richness. ## Reflections What I like about GoogLeNet is how “smart” it feels. Instead of just going bigger and deeper like VGG, it asked: can we be more efficient? And it worked. With far fewer parameters, it still won ImageNet. It also introduced ideas that carried forward. The use of 1×1 convolutions was picked up by later models. Global average pooling is standard today. Even the idea of modular design echoes in ResNet and beyond. GoogLeNet proved that CNNs didn’t have to be brute force. You could design architectures that were both deep and efficient. This was a lesson that shaped the next wave of models.

document.title: LeNet – The First CNN That Started It All
document.description: Exploring LeNet, one of the earliest convolutional neural networks that laid the foundation for modern deep learning.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation When I think about where to start with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), it feels natural to begin with LeNet. This was the first real CNN that worked, built by Yann LeCun back in the 1990s and introduced in the paper *Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition*. And honestly, it’s also the first model I ever saw in a class when we switched from fully connected networks to image tasks. So it holds a bit of a “first step” feeling for me. At that time, people were trying to get computers to recognize handwritten digits, like the numbers on checks or zip codes on letters. The common approach was to design features by hand. These features included things like edge detectors, strokes, or corners. But handwriting is messy. People slant their digits, change the size, write quickly or slowly. Hand-crafted features just couldn’t handle all that variation. LeNet’s big idea was: what if the network *learns* those features directly from pixels? No manual feature engineering. Just raw 28×28 images of digits from the MNIST dataset, and let the network figure out edges, curves, and shapes on its own. That feels obvious to us now, but back then it was a huge shift. What surprised me when I first revisited this paper is how much of today’s CNN structure was already there: convolution layers to detect patterns, pooling to downsample, and fully connected layers at the end to do the classification. Even though the network looks tiny compared to models we use now, the blueprint was basically the same. So in this post, I want to walk through LeNet step by step. I’ll break down the architecture layer by layer, explain why they made the choices they did, and also show some PyTorch code for it. My hope is that if you’ve never seen a CNN before, this will feel like a clear and approachable first example. ## Architecture Breakdown Here’s where LeNet gets interesting. It might look small, but it’s built from the same building blocks that modern CNNs still use today. Think of it as the blueprint. ### Input The network takes in a 32×32 grayscale image. MNIST digits are 28×28, so the authors padded them to 32×32. Nothing fancy here, just making the math easier. ### First Convolution (C1) The first layer applies 6 filters of size 5×5. Each filter is like a stencil sliding over the image, picking out edges or curves. You end up with 6 new images (feature maps) that highlight different patterns. ### First Pooling (S2) Then comes average pooling. Imagine squinting at the image so small details blur out, but the big shapes stay visible. This reduces the size from 28×28 to 14×14. ### Second Convolution (C3) Now 16 new filters scan these smaller maps. This time the filters look for more complex shapes, like combinations of edges forming corners or loops. ### Second Pooling (S4) Another average pooling step, shrinking things down again. At this point the network is no longer staring at pixels, it’s staring at patterns of strokes and shapes. ### Third Convolution (C5) This layer uses 120 filters that cover the entire 5×5 maps. Each filter basically compresses a whole map into one number. Think of it as summarizing everything it’s seen so far into a set of key signals. ### Fully Connected (F6) and Output Finally, the model uses two fully connected layers. The first has 84 neurons, the second has 10 outputs (digits 0–9). This part is like a traditional neural network classifier, taking all the learned features and turning them into a prediction. --- Two things stand out: 1. Pooling was average pooling, not max pooling. Max pooling came later and is now more common. 2. Activations were tanh, not ReLU. ReLU was introduced much later with AlexNet in 2012. Even though LeNet is tiny compared to modern CNNs, the pattern is the same: convolution → pooling → convolution → pooling → fully connected → output. Once you understand this, bigger models like AlexNet and VGG make a lot more sense — they just add depth and scale. ## Implementation Notes To get a better feel for LeNet, I coded it out in PyTorch. Here’s a simplified version: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class LeNet5(nn.Module): def __init__(self): super(LeNet5, self).__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, kernel_size=5) # C1 self.pool1 = nn.AvgPool2d(2, stride=2) # S2 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, kernel_size=5) # C3 self.pool2 = nn.AvgPool2d(2, stride=2) # S4 self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(16, 120, kernel_size=5) # C5 self.fc1 = nn.Linear(120, 84) # F6 self.fc2 = nn.Linear(84, 10) # Output def forward(self, x): x = torch.tanh(self.conv1(x)) x = self.pool1(x) x = torch.tanh(self.conv2(x)) x = self.pool2(x) x = torch.tanh(self.conv3(x)) x = x.view(-1, 120) x = torch.tanh(self.fc1(x)) x = self.fc2(x) return x ``` I used tanh activations and average pooling to stay close to the original design. Out of curiosity, I tried swapping them for ReLU and max pooling, and the model performed better. That small test shows how later innovations didn’t reinvent CNNs, they just refined the same blueprint. Training this model on MNIST was fast and straightforward. On my machine it takes seconds, but it’s crazy to think that back in the 90s this was pushing the limits of compute. What feels like a toy model today was once cutting-edge. ## Why the Design Choices Matter One of the things I like about LeNet is that you can actually see the reasoning behind each design choice. **Convolutions over fully connected layers** If you tried to use a fully connected layer on a 32×32 image, you’d end up with thousands of weights right away. Convolutions solve that by reusing the same small filter everywhere, which keeps parameters manageable and also makes the network look for patterns across the whole image. **Pooling layers** Pooling is like zooming out. You lose a little detail but gain robustness. A digit shifted by a pixel or two still looks like the same digit after pooling, which helps with invariance. **Tanh activations** Today, we almost always use ReLU, but back then tanh was the standard. It squashes values into the range [-1, 1], which made optimization easier with the tools they had at the time. It’s slower than ReLU, but it got the job done. **Average pooling vs max pooling** LeNet used average pooling, which smooths things out. Nowadays max pooling is more common since it keeps the strongest signal. My guess is that average pooling felt more stable in the 90s, and computation was a big factor too. --- Seeing these choices in context makes me realize that nothing about modern CNNs is “magical.” The ideas were already here — we just changed the details as hardware and training methods improved. ## Reflections ## Reflections and What Came Next LeNet might look small today, but it showed me how powerful CNNs really are. Convolutions to find edges, pooling to simplify, and fully connected layers to make the final call — that recipe is still everywhere. What I found surprising is how many choices were different from what we’d use now. Tanh instead of ReLU, average pooling instead of max pooling. When I swapped those in my own code, training felt faster and accuracy improved. It made me realize later models weren’t doing something entirely new, just refining LeNet’s blueprint. And that blueprint carried forward. AlexNet scaled it up with GPUs and ReLU. VGG went deeper. GoogLeNet made it efficient. ResNet added skip connections. If you squint, they all still look like LeNet. That’s why this model feels like the “hello world” of CNNs — simple, but it gives you the mental map to understand everything that came after.

document.title: MobileNet — Lightweight CNNs for Mobile Devices
document.description: Breaking down MobileNet, the model that introduced depthwise separable convolutions to make CNNs efficient enough for mobile and embedded systems.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation Up until ResNet, the trend was clear: deeper, bigger, more accurate. That’s great if you have massive GPUs, but what if you want to run a CNN on your phone or an IoT device? That’s where **MobileNet** comes in. Published by Google in 2017, MobileNet showed how to make CNNs efficient without losing too much accuracy. The key idea was the **depthwise separable convolution**, which reduces the computations of a normal convolution by almost a factor of 8–9×. That’s what made MobileNet small and fast enough for real-time applications like image classification on mobile devices. ## Architecture Breakdown The big idea in MobileNet is the **depthwise separable convolution**. To understand why it matters, let’s first look at a regular convolution. ### Standard convolution In a normal 3×3 convolution with, say, 32 filters on an input with 32 channels, each filter is 3×3×32 in size. That means every filter looks across all channels at once, and we apply 32 of them. The math adds up fast — about 9×32×32 operations per pixel location. That’s powerful, but also expensive. ### Step 1: Depthwise convolution MobileNet splits this into two parts. First comes the **depthwise convolution**. Instead of each filter looking at *all* channels, it applies one filter per channel. If the input has 32 channels, we use 32 separate 3×3 filters, one for each channel. That way, each channel is processed independently. This captures spatial patterns (edges, textures) inside each channel, but doesn’t mix information *between* channels yet. ### Step 2: Pointwise convolution Next comes the **pointwise convolution**, which is just a 1×1 convolution. This layer mixes information across the channels. You can think of it as combining the independent channel-wise features learned in the depthwise step. The pointwise step is what lets the network build richer representations after the cheap depthwise step. ### Why this matters Together, these two steps approximate what a full convolution does, but with far fewer operations. For example: - Standard 3×3 conv on 256 channels with 256 filters: ~590k multiplications. - Depthwise (3×3 per channel) + pointwise (1×1 mixing): ~69k multiplications. That’s nearly an **8–9× reduction** in computation, with only a small drop in accuracy. ### MobileNet v1 design The original MobileNet v1 is basically a stack of these depthwise separable conv blocks. Every block has: - Depthwise conv (3×3) → BatchNorm → ReLU - Pointwise conv (1×1) → BatchNorm → ReLU The network is deep but light, and at the end it uses average pooling and a fully connected layer for classification. ### Width and resolution multipliers On top of this, MobileNet added two clever “knobs” for trading off speed and accuracy: - **Width multiplier (α):** scales the number of channels in every layer. If α < 1, the network gets thinner (fewer channels, fewer computations). For example, α=0.5 halves the number of channels everywhere. - **Resolution multiplier (ρ):** scales the input image size. Training and running at 160×160 instead of 224×224 makes the network much faster, though accuracy drops a bit. These multipliers gave developers flexibility. You could pick a smaller MobileNet for a phone, or a bigger one for a more powerful device. It made the architecture practical outside of research labs. ## Why the Design Choices Matter **Efficiency over brute force** Instead of stacking more layers like VGG or ResNet, MobileNet was about doing more with less. This made it practical for edge devices. **Depthwise separable convs** This was the game changer. They became a staple not just in MobileNet but in later models like Xception and EfficientNet. **Multipliers (α, ρ)** This gave developers flexibility. Depending on the device, you could shrink the network to run faster, or keep it larger for accuracy. --- ## Implementation Notes Let’s build MobileNet step by step in PyTorch. The key is to start with the core idea — depthwise separable convolutions — and then show how that idea becomes the actual MobileNet blocks. Along the way, we’ll also cover width and resolution multipliers. ### Step 1: Depthwise Separable Convolution At the heart of MobileNet is the depthwise separable convolution. To make the concept clear, let’s write a minimal version: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class DepthwiseSeparableConv(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1): super(DepthwiseSeparableConv, self).__init__() # depthwise: one 3x3 filter per input channel self.depthwise = nn.Conv2d( in_channels, in_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, groups=in_channels, bias=False ) # pointwise: 1x1 conv mixes across channels self.pointwise = nn.Conv2d( in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1, bias=False ) self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) def forward(self, x): x = self.depthwise(x) x = self.pointwise(x) x = self.bn(x) x = self.relu(x) return x ``` This block is useful for teaching. You can literally see how a normal convolution is broken into a depthwise step (spatial features in each channel) and a pointwise step (channel mixing). That’s the core idea. ### Step 2: MobileNet Block In practice, MobileNet doesn’t use the minimal version above directly. Each stage also includes batch norm and ReLU after both depthwise and pointwise convolutions. Let’s wrap that into a MobileNetBlock: ```python class MobileNetBlock(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1): super(MobileNetBlock, self).__init__() self.block = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels, in_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, groups=in_channels, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(in_channels), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), ) def forward(self, x): return self.block(x) ``` This is the version that gets stacked over and over again to form MobileNet v1. ### Step 3: Width Multiplier (α) One of the clever tricks in MobileNet is the width multiplier (α). It scales the number of channels across the whole network. If α < 1, you get a thinner, faster model. If α > 1, you get a wider, more accurate one. ```python def adjust_channels(channels, alpha): return max(1, int(channels * alpha)) # Example: cut channels in half print(adjust_channels(32, alpha=0.5)) # 16 ``` This simple scaling gives you a family of MobileNets instead of a single fixed network. ### Step 4: Resolution Multiplier (ρ) Unlike α, the resolution multiplier (ρ) isn’t coded into the network. Instead, it’s applied to the input image size. Smaller inputs → faster network, but less accuracy. ```python from torchvision import transforms rho = 0.75 # resolution multiplier base_size = 224 input_size = int(base_size * rho) transform = transforms.Compose([ transforms.Resize((input_size, input_size)), transforms.ToTensor(), ]) ``` So α thins the network, while ρ shrinks the inputs. Put together, they let you tune MobileNet for whatever device you’re running on. ### Step 5: Tiny MobileNet Now we can put it all together. Here’s a small demo version of MobileNet that uses MobileNetBlock and the width multiplier: ```python class TinyMobileNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, alpha=1.0, num_classes=1000): super(TinyMobileNet, self).__init__() def c(ch): return adjust_channels(ch, alpha) self.features = nn.Sequential( MobileNetBlock(3, c(32), stride=2), MobileNetBlock(c(32), c(64), stride=1), MobileNetBlock(c(64), c(128), stride=2), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), ) self.classifier = nn.Linear(c(128), num_classes) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) return self.classifier(x) ``` This isn’t the full MobileNet v1, but it demonstrates all the important parts: depthwise separable convs, stacked blocks, width multipliers, and resolution multipliers. By building it piece by piece, you can see how MobileNet went from a single idea (split convolutions) to a full architecture that was efficient enough to run on phones and edge devices. ##Reflections and What Came Next What I like about MobileNet is that it shifted the focus from “accuracy at any cost” to “accuracy that fits in your pocket.” It showed that CNNs weren’t just for labs with GPUs — they could actually run on real-world devices. Later versions built on this. MobileNetV2 added inverted residual blocks with linear bottlenecks. MobileNetV3 combined these with ideas from neural architecture search (NAS). Together, they’ve become the go-to backbones for mobile and embedded vision tasks. For me, MobileNet is a reminder that deep learning isn’t just about getting the best accuracy. It’s about finding the right balance of speed, memory, and performance for where the model will run.

document.title: R-CNN — Regions with CNN Features
document.description: Breaking down the original R-CNN paper (2014), which combined region proposals with deep CNN features to push object detection far beyond the traditional methods like HOG and DPM.

body.raw:
## Context & Motivation

Up to this point in the timeline, most of the progress
we’ve talked about has been on **image classification**.
Models like AlexNet and VGG could look at a picture and
tell you what was in it - cat, dog, car, airplane. That was
impressive, but it wasn’t enough for a lot of real-world
applications.

Take **object detection** as an example. Instead of just
answering *“is there a dog in this image?”*, we also need
to answer *“where exactly is the dog?”*. That means the
model has to output not just a label but also **bounding
boxes** around the objects in the picture.

This step from classification to detection was a huge
challenge. Why? Because you don’t know in advance how
many objects are in an image, where they are, or how big
they might be. A single photo could have one large object,
like a car, or it could have many small ones, like people
in a crowd. The detector has to find them all.

---

### What came before R-CNN

Before deep learning took over, people used **hand-crafted
features** like SIFT, HOG, or Haar cascades combined with
shallow classifiers such as SVMs or boosted decision
trees. These worked for simple tasks like face detection
(Haar cascades were used in early versions of OpenCV), but
they didn’t scale well to complex datasets.

The more advanced version of this was the **Deformable
Parts Model (DPM)**. DPMs broke objects into parts (like a
car = wheels + body + windows), each with its own detector
that could deform a little bit. This was the state of the
art on datasets like PASCAL VOC before CNNs showed up. But
the performance of these methods had plateaued. They just
weren’t improving much.

---

### Why not just use CNNs directly?

At this point (around 2013–2014), CNNs like AlexNet had
already proven themselves on classification. So the
natural idea was: *why not just run a CNN everywhere in
the image and find objects that way?*

The problem was **computational cost**. Running a CNN on
every possible location, at every possible scale, across
an image would take forever. People tried this with
“sliding window” methods, but it was painfully slow and
impractical.

---

### The key problem

So the field was stuck between two bad options:
1. **Classical methods** like HOG + SVM or DPM: fast
   enough, but accuracy was plateauing.
2. **Naive CNN sliding windows**: accurate in principle,
   but far too slow to be usable.

What we needed was a way to **combine CNN features with
detection** in a way that was both accurate *and* at least
somewhat practical. That’s where **R-CNN (Regions with
CNN features)** comes in. It introduced a clever pipeline
that bridged this gap: use region proposals to narrow down
where objects might be, then run CNNs only on those
regions.

This idea kicked off an entire family of models — Fast
R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN — but it all started here.

## Main Idea of R-CNN

The breakthrough in R-CNN (Regions with CNN features) was
realizing that you don’t need to run a CNN across every
possible location in the image. Instead, you first **propose
a small set of candidate regions** that are likely to
contain objects, and then run a CNN only on those.

The pipeline had five main steps:

---

### 1. Region Proposals
Instead of sliding a window everywhere, R-CNN used a
classical computer vision method called **Selective
Search**. This algorithm looks at the image, groups
similar pixels into regions, and proposes about **2000
candidate bounding boxes** that might contain objects.
The key insight: it’s much cheaper to check 2000 boxes
than millions of sliding windows.

---

### 2. Warping Regions
CNNs (like AlexNet) expect a fixed input size, but the
region proposals all come in different shapes and sizes.
So each proposed region is **warped into a fixed 227×227
image** before feeding it to the CNN. This step made the
pipeline clunky but necessary, since CNNs couldn’t handle
variable input shapes.

---

### 3. CNN Feature Extraction
Each warped region is passed through a CNN (in the
original paper, they fine-tuned **AlexNet** on PASCAL VOC).
Instead of using the final classification output, they
take the activations from one of the fully connected
layers as a **feature vector**. These CNN features turned
out to be far more powerful than hand-crafted features
like HOG.

---

### 4. Classification with SVMs
Once you have features for each region, you still need
to decide what’s inside. R-CNN trained a set of
**class-specific SVM classifiers** (one per object class).
Each SVM takes the CNN features and predicts whether the
region contains, say, a dog, a car, or nothing at all.

---

### 5. Bounding Box Regression
The last step fixes localization. The region proposals
from Selective Search are rough — they often don’t line
up perfectly with the object. So R-CNN adds a simple
**bounding box regressor** (a linear regression model)
that shifts and scales the box to better fit the object.

---

### Putting it Together
So the full R-CNN pipeline looked like this:

1. Generate ~2000 region proposals with Selective Search.  
2. Warp each region to 227×227.  
3. Extract features using a CNN.  
4. Classify with SVMs.  
5. Refine the bounding box with regression.  

It was a multi-stage system, a bit clunky, but it worked
shockingly well compared to anything before it. On the
PASCAL VOC benchmark, R-CNN blew past traditional
detectors like HOG + SVM or DPM, and it became the
blueprint for the next generation of detectors.


## Main Idea of R-CNN

The breakthrough in R-CNN (Regions with CNN features) was
realizing that you don’t need to run a CNN across every
possible location in the image. Instead, you first **propose
a small set of candidate regions** that are likely to
contain objects, and then run a CNN only on those.

The pipeline had five main steps:

---

### 1. Region Proposals

than millions of sliding windows.

---

### 2. Warping Regions

region proposals all come in different shapes and sizes.
So each proposed region is **warped into a fixed 227×227
image** before feeding it to the CNN. This step made the
pipeline clunky but necessary, since CNNs couldn’t handle
variable input shapes.

---

### 3. CNN Feature Extraction
Each warped region is passed through a CNN (in the
original paper, they fine-tuned **AlexNet** on PASCAL VOC).
Instead of using the final classification output, they
take the activations from one of the fully connected

out to be far more powerful than hand-crafted features
like HOG.

---

### 4. Classification with SVMs
Once you have features for each region, you still need
to decide what’s inside. R-CNN trained a set of

Each SVM takes the CNN features and predicts whether the
region contains, say, a dog, a car, or nothing at all.

---

### 5. Bounding Box Regression
The last step fixes localization. The region proposals
from Selective Search are rough — they often don’t line
up perfectly with the object. So R-CNN adds a simple
**bounding box regressor** (a linear regression model)
that shifts and scales the box to better fit the object.

---

### Putting it Together
So the full R-CNN pipeline looked like this:

1. Generate ~2000 region proposals with Selective Search.  
2. Warp each region to 227×227.  
3. Extract features using a CNN.  
4. Classify with SVMs.  
5. Refine the bounding box with regression.  

It was a multi-stage system, a bit clunky, but it worked
shockingly well compared to anything before it. On the
PASCAL VOC benchmark, R-CNN blew past traditional
detectors like HOG + SVM or DPM, and it became the
blueprint for the next generation of detectors.

---

### Step 3: CNN Feature Extraction

Once all the region proposals are warped to 227×227,
they’re ready to be passed into a CNN. In the original
R-CNN, the authors used **AlexNet**, which had just won
ImageNet in 2012. This was one of the first times CNNs
were used for detection, not just classification.

But here’s the important part: R-CNN didn’t use AlexNet’s
final classification layer (the softmax). Instead, it took
the activations from the **second fully connected layer**
(fc7). This layer outputs a **4096-dimensional feature
vector**, which serves as a rich description of the region.

Why not just keep AlexNet’s softmax output? Because that
softmax was trained for **classification** on ImageNet
(1000 classes). For detection, we need something more
flexible. By using fc7 as a feature extractor, R-CNN could
pair those features with its own classifiers trained on
detection datasets like PASCAL VOC.

Another detail worth noting: to make training practical,
R-CNN didn’t keep running AlexNet on-the-fly during SVM
training. Instead, they ran all 2000 proposals per image
through AlexNet once, saved the 4096-D features to disk,
and then trained SVMs offline. This caching step worked,
but it required **hundreds of gigabytes of storage**. It
was one of the practical bottlenecks of the approach.

---

### Step 4: SVM Classification

Once we have CNN features for each region, the next step
is deciding what’s inside the box. Instead of retraining
AlexNet’s built-in classifier, R-CNN trained a set of
**linear SVMs** — one per object class.

Here’s how it worked:

- Suppose we’re detecting 20 object categories (like in
  PASCAL VOC). R-CNN trained **20 different SVMs**, one
  for each class.  
- Each SVM takes the 4096-D feature vector from AlexNet’s
  fc7 layer. The first decides *is this a car?*. The next decides *is this a dog?*. The next decides *is
  this a person?*  
- Any region that doesn’t strongly match one of these
  SVMs is classified as **background**.

Why SVMs instead of a softmax? At the time, SVMs were
popular because they worked well with limited training
data and gave sharp decision boundaries. Plus, the
community was already familiar with SVM-based object
detectors (like HOG + SVM), so the idea felt natural.

The downside was complexity. This created a **multi-stage
training pipeline**:  
1. Fine-tune AlexNet on detection data.  
2. Extract features for every proposal.  
3. Train separate SVMs on top of those features.  

It wasn’t end-to-end like modern detectors, but it was a
clever way to combine CNN feature learning with classical
classification methods.

---

### Step 5: Bounding Box Regression

Even after Selective Search finds regions and the SVMs
classify them, there’s still one issue: **the boxes aren’t
always tight**. Selective Search might put a box around a
dog, but it could be shifted slightly to the left or cut
off part of the tail. For good detection, we need precise
localization.

To fix this, R-CNN added a lightweight **bounding box
regression module**:

- **Input:** the same 4096-D CNN features (from AlexNet’s
  fc7 layer).  
- **Output:** four numbers (Δx, Δy, Δw, Δh) that represent
  adjustments to the box’s position (x, y) and size (w, h).  
- **Training:** for each class, a separate linear regressor
  is trained to predict these offsets so the box aligns
  better with the ground truth.

This step may sound small, but it made a noticeable
difference. Without it, detections were often rough. With
it, the boxes became tighter and more accurate.

---

### Putting It All Together

Now we can see the full R-CNN pipeline in action:

1. **Selective Search** proposes ~2000 regions per image.  
2. **Warping** resizes each region to 227×227.  
3. **CNN features** are extracted from AlexNet’s fc7 layer.  
4. **SVMs** classify each region into an object category or
   background.  
5. **Bounding box regression** refines the boxes for better
   localization.  

This was a **multi-stage pipeline**, with each part trained
separately: CNN fine-tuning, feature extraction, SVM
training, and regression training. It wasn’t fast, and it
wasn’t elegant — but it worked better than anything before
it. On PASCAL VOC, R-CNN crushed traditional detectors like
HOG + SVM and Deformable Parts Models, marking the start of
the deep learning era in object detection.

## Why This Was Important (and Its Limitations)

R-CNN marked a turning point in object detection. On the
PASCAL VOC benchmark, it improved mean average precision
from about **30% with DPMs** to over **50%**. That was a
huge jump — the kind of breakthrough that made everyone
pay attention to CNNs.

It proved three key things:  
- **CNNs work for detection.** Until then, they were mostly
  used for classification.  
- **Hybrid pipelines can succeed.** By mixing Selective
  Search, CNN features, and SVMs, R-CNN bridged the gap
  between classical and deep learning methods.  
- **There was room to grow.** Its clunky design highlighted
  the path forward.

But R-CNN also came with big drawbacks:  
- **Slow:** ~2000 proposals per image, each passed through
  a CNN. Processing one image could take minutes.  
- **Multi-stage training:** CNN fine-tuning, SVMs, and box
  regressors all trained separately.  
- **Storage heavy:** features for proposals were cached to
  disk, taking up hundreds of gigabytes.  

So R-CNN was both a breakthrough *and* a bottleneck. It
changed the conversation — detection was now about CNNs —
but it also made it clear that faster, end-to-end methods
were needed. That challenge is exactly what led to **Fast
R-CNN** and beyond.

## Implementation Notes

R-CNN was a multi-stage pipeline. To make sense of it, let’s
build it up piece by piece in PyTorch. This won’t be a full
reproduction of the paper (since the real system had a lot
of moving parts), but it will capture the main ideas.

---

### Step 1: Region Proposals with Selective Search

The first step is generating candidate boxes. In practice,
R-CNN used **Selective Search**, which isn’t built into
PyTorch, but there are Python implementations we can call.

Here’s a minimal way to run Selective Search with
`scikit-image`:

```python
import skimage.data
import skimage.segmentation
import selectivesearch

def get_region_proposals(image):
    # run selective search
    img_lbl, regions = selectivesearch.selective_search(
        image, scale=500, sigma=0.9, min_size=10
    )
    candidates = set()
    for r in regions:
        if r['rect'] in candidates:
            continue
        x, y, w, h = r['rect']
        # skip small or oddly sized boxes
        if w < 20 or h < 20:
            continue
        candidates.add((x, y, w, h))
    return list(candidates)
```

This gives us a list of bounding boxes (x, y, w, h).
Typically, you’d keep around 2000 per image.

###Step 2: Warping Regions

Each box comes in different sizes. R-CNN warped them into
227×227 crops so they could be passed through AlexNet.

```python
import torch
import torchvision.transforms as T
from PIL import Image

transform = T.Compose([
    T.Resize((227, 227)),
    T.ToTensor(),
])

def crop_and_warp(image, box):
    x, y, w, h = box
    region = image[y:y+h, x:x+w]
    region_pil = Image.fromarray(region)
    return transform(region_pil).unsqueeze(0)  # add batch dim
```

This step introduces distortion but makes the inputs
compatible with the CNN.

### Step 3: CNN Feature Extraction

R-CNN used AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on
VOC. Instead of the softmax output, they took features from
the fc7 layer.

Here’s how we can do that with PyTorch’s AlexNet:

```python
import torchvision.models as models
import torch.nn as nn

alexnet = models.alexnet(pretrained=True)
# remove final classifier, keep up to fc7
feature_extractor = nn.Sequential(*list(alexnet.classifier.children())[:-1])

def extract_features(region_tensor):
    # pass through AlexNet (features + fc7)
    with torch.no_grad():
        feats = alexnet.features(region_tensor)
        feats = feats.view(feats.size(0), -1)
        feats = feature_extractor(feats)
    return feats  # 4096-D vector
```

Each region proposal now becomes a 4096-dimensional
vector.

### Step 4: SVM Classification

Once we have CNN features, we train linear SVMs (one per
class) to classify each region.

```python
from sklearn import svm

# Suppose we have feature vectors and labels
X = [...]  # list of 4096-D feature vectors
y = [...]  # labels: car, dog, person, etc.

clf = svm.LinearSVC()
clf.fit(X, y)
```

At test time, each region’s CNN features are passed into
the SVMs to predict its class.

### Step 5: Bounding Box Regression

Finally, to refine localization, R-CNN added a bounding box
regressor. This is just a linear regression model that
predicts offsets to make the boxes tighter.

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Train per class with CNN features as input
regressor = LinearRegression()
regressor.fit(X, deltas)  # deltas = [dx, dy, dw, dh]
```

At test time, the predicted offsets adjust the candidate
box to better fit the object.

### Putting It Together

So the workflow looks like this:

1. Run Selective Search to get candidate boxes.
2. Warp each box to 227×227.
3. Extract CNN features (fc7) from AlexNet.
4. Classify with SVMs.
5. Refine boxes with regression.

Each part had to be trained separately — which made R-CNN
slow and storage-heavy — but this pipeline was the first to
show that CNN features could crush traditional detectors.

## Reflections and What Came Next

What stands out to me about R-CNN is how much it feels
like a bridge between two worlds. On one side, you have
the old-school computer vision tricks like Selective
Search and SVMs. On the other, you have deep CNNs like
AlexNet. R-CNN glued them together, and that glue was
enough to change the field.

Reading about it today, the design almost feels clunky.
Running a CNN 2000 times per image, saving hundreds of
gigabytes of features, training SVMs and regressors
separately. It’s not elegant. But in 2014, it was a
proof of concept that CNN features were powerful enough
to replace hand-crafted ones. That proof was all the
community needed.

The other thing I learned is how research often moves.
You don’t jump from “bad detection” to “perfect detection”
in one step. R-CNN solved the accuracy problem but left
behind big speed and efficiency problems. Those exact
pain points directly led to **Fast R-CNN** and then
**Faster R-CNN**. Each version fixed one bottleneck until
the pipeline became fast, end-to-end, and practical.

So while R-CNN itself is rarely used today, it’s the
ancestor of almost every detector that came after. For
me, it’s a reminder that sometimes the “clunky first

document.title: ResNet – Solving the Depth Problem
document.description: Exploring ResNet, the residual network that introduced skip connections and made training very deep models possible.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation By 2015, the trend was clear: deeper networks kept winning ImageNet. AlexNet had 8 layers, VGG stretched that to 16 and 19, and GoogLeNet managed 22 with clever modules. But there was a problem: when people tried to go even deeper, training actually got worse. Adding more layers sometimes increased the training error, which didn’t make sense at first. ResNet, introduced by Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research, solved this with a simple but brilliant idea: **residual connections** (a.k.a. skip connections). Instead of forcing each layer to learn a full transformation, they let the layer just learn the difference (the residual). This made training much easier and suddenly networks with 50, 101, or even 152 layers became possible. When I first read about ResNet, it stood out because of how minimal the change was, yet how big the impact turned out to be. A single skip connection redefined the way deep networks were built. ## Model Breakdown The core building block is the **residual block**. Instead of just stacking convolutions, ResNet adds the input back to the output: Input → [Conv → BN → ReLU → Conv → BN] → Add skip connection → ReLU - If input and output dimensions match, the input is added directly. - If they differ, a 1×1 convolution is used to align dimensions. This skip connection allows gradients to flow backward more easily during training, solving the vanishing gradient problem. ### Variants - **ResNet18/34**: Basic blocks with two 3×3 convolutions. - **ResNet50/101/152**: Bottleneck blocks (1×1 → 3×3 → 1×1 convolutions). ResNet152 had 152 layers but was trainable, something that was previously impossible with plain CNNs. It won the 2015 ImageNet competition with a top-5 error rate of 3.57%, surpassing human-level performance. ## Why the Design Choices Matter **Skip connections** These were the magic ingredient. By letting information skip over layers, the network could go much deeper without losing the signal. **Bottleneck design** For deeper versions, the 1×1 convolutions acted like compression layers, reducing computation while still keeping depth. **Normalization** Batch Normalization (BN) was critical here too. Combined with skip connections, it made very deep training stable. --- ## Implementation Notes Here’s a simplified PyTorch version of a basic residual block: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class BasicBlock(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1): super(BasicBlock, self).__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) self.shortcut = nn.Sequential() if stride != 1 or in_channels != out_channels: self.shortcut = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) ) def forward(self, x): out = self.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x))) out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out)) out += self.shortcut(x) out = self.relu(out) return out ``` What struck me when coding this was how natural the skip connection feels. Adding the input back to the output doesn’t add much complexity but changes training dynamics completely. When I trained a small ResNet on CIFAR10, it converged more reliably than a plain deep CNN of similar size. ## Reflections What I love about ResNet is how small the change was. Just add a shortcut, and suddenly 152-layer networks were trainable. It’s the kind of idea that feels obvious in hindsight but was groundbreaking at the time. The influence of ResNet is everywhere. Modern CNNs, object detectors, and even Transformers all use some form of residual connection. It turned out that this “simple skip” wasn’t just a hack — it became a core design principle. ResNet showed me that sometimes progress in deep learning isn’t about making things more complicated. It’s about making training easier, so depth and scale can do the heavy lifting.

document.title: VGG – Simplicity in Depth
document.description: Exploring VGG, the architecture that showed depth and uniform design could improve performance on large-scale image recognition.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation By 2014, AlexNet had already proven that CNNs could crush image classification when scaled up, and GoogLeNet was experimenting with clever modules to make things efficient. VGG, from the Visual Geometry Group at Oxford (hence the name), took a different path. Instead of being fancy, it asked a simple question: *what if we just make the network deeper, but keep it uniform?* That idea sounds obvious now, but it was powerful. VGG showed that depth alone, combined with small 3×3 filters, could significantly improve performance on ImageNet. This was also one of the first models that people outside research used heavily for transfer learning, since its structure was clean and easy to adapt. When I first learned about VGG in class, it was presented as the "clean" architecture. It looked boring compared to GoogLeNet or ResNet, but that’s what made it so influential. The simplicity was its strength. ## Model Breakdown The most popular versions are **VGG16** and **VGG19**, where the numbers stand for how many weight layers they have. The structure looks repetitive, but that was the point: stack small 3×3 convolutions, add a pooling layer, repeat, and then finish with a few fully connected layers. Here’s the pattern for **VGG16**: - Input: 224×224 RGB image - Conv3-64 → Conv3-64 → MaxPool - Conv3-128 → Conv3-128 → MaxPool - Conv3-256 → Conv3-256 → Conv3-256 → MaxPool - Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → MaxPool - Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → Conv3-512 → MaxPool - FC-4096 → FC-4096 → FC-1000 (softmax) The main differences from AlexNet: - All conv filters are 3×3 with stride 1, padding 1 - Pooling is always 2×2 with stride 2 - Deeper, more consistent design (16–19 layers) --- ## Why the Design Choices Matter **3×3 convolutions** Stacking two 3×3 convs gives you the receptive field of a 5×5 filter, but with fewer parameters and more non-linearities. This made the network expressive without exploding in size. **Depth** Before VGG, CNNs were usually under 10 layers. VGG pushed this to 16 and 19 layers, showing that deeper really was better (as long as you had data and compute). **Uniform design** Because every block looked the same, it was easy to reason about and extend. This is why VGG quickly became a go-to backbone for other tasks like detection and segmentation. --- ## Implementation Notes Here’s a simplified PyTorch version of VGG16: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class VGG16(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes=1000): super(VGG16, self).__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( # Block 1 nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 2 nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(128, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 3 nn.Conv2d(128, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 4 nn.Conv2d(256, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), # Block 5 nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Conv2d(512, 512, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True), nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2), ) self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(512 * 7 * 7, 4096), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, 4096), nn.ReLU(True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) x = self.classifier(x) return x ``` Training VGG was much more computationally expensive than AlexNet. It highlighted the need for faster GPUs and more memory. Despite that, it became hugely popular in research, especially for transfer learning on smaller datasets. ## Reflections What I like about VGG is how straightforward it is. Compared to GoogLeNet’s Inception modules or ResNet’s skip connections, VGG is just stack, pool, stack, pool. That simplicity made it a great teaching model and a backbone for lots of other tasks. Of course, it came at a cost. VGG16 has about 138 million parameters, which is huge compared to modern networks. It’s heavy and not very efficient. But it proved the point: depth and uniform design worked. Later models built on this lesson. ResNet solved the training difficulties that came with even deeper networks. EfficientNet explored better scaling rules. Transformers went in a totally new direction. But VGG’s fingerprint is still visible in many of them: small filters, repeated blocks, and the idea that simple can sometimes beat clever.

`,(0,n.jsxDEV)(e.p,{children:`Later models built on this lesson. ResNet solved the training difficulties that
came with even deeper networks. EfficientNet explored better scaling rules.

document.title: Vision Transformers Explained
document.description: A breakdown of how ViTs process images as sequences.

body.raw:
Vision Transformers (ViTs) treat an image as a sequence of patches and apply
the Transformer encoder architecture.

## Patch embedding

Split an image into fixed-size patches and linearly project each to an embedding.

```python
import torch

def patchify(img, patch_size=16):
    b, c, h, w = img.shape
    ph = pw = patch_size
    img = img.view(b, c, h // ph, ph, w // pw, pw)
    return img.permute(0, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1).contiguous().view(b, -1, ph*pw*c)
```

## Self-attention

Each token attends to all others, capturing global context in a single layer.
